title: Visual perception of materials and their properties

findings.consequent: Perception of materials (via statistical generative models capturing natural appearance variation)
findings.source: abstract
findings.quote: visual system does not actually estimate physical parameters of materials and objects. Instead—I argue—the brain is remarkably adept at building 'statistical generative models' that capture the natural degrees of variation in appearance between samples.

findings.antecedent: Low- and mid-level image measurements (e.g., specular reflections)
findings.source: abstract
findings.quote: when determining perceived glossiness, the brain does not estimate parameters of the BRDF. Instead, it uses a constellation of low- and mid-level image measurements to characterize the extent to which the surface manifests specular reflections.

findings.antecedent: Visual distinction of materials and properties
findings.consequent: Utility for tasks (e.g., determining edibility, selecting foot/handholds)
findings.source: 1. Background
findings.quote: Being able to visually distinguish between materials and infer their properties by sight, is invaluable for many tasks.

findings.source: 1. Background
findings.quote: subjects can identify a wide range of materials from photographs even with brief presentations.

findings.source: 1. Background
findings.quote: subjective ratings of the individual samples were systematically clustered into categories, suggesting that subjects could theoretically classify materials through visual judgments of their properties.

findings.antecedent: Photographs of real vs. fake materials (brief presentations)
findings.source: 1. Background
findings.quote: subjects were able to make remarkably precise descriptions of the properties of materials and were above chance performance at distinguishing between real and fake materials.

findings.source: 1. Background
findings.quote: this ability generalizes across differences in lighting, as long as the illumination has statistical structure that is typical of the natural environment.

findings.source: 1. Background
findings.quote: varying the statistical characteristics of the illumination has systematic effects on perceived glossiness, which can be predicted from the low-level properties of the image.

findings.antecedent: Binocular disparity, motion information, highlight properties (brightness, position, orientation relative to diffuse shading)
findings.source: 1. Background
findings.quote: Judgments of specular reflectance are affected by both binocular disparity and motion information... as well as the properties of highlights, including their brightness, position and orientation relative to diffuse shading on the surface.

findings.source: 1. Background
findings.quote: increasing the skewness of images of matte stucco reliefs made the surfaces appear glossy.

findings.source: 1. Background
findings.quote: skewness is neither necessary nor sufficient to predict perceived glossiness, and have called into question the idea that such simple image statistics could account for surface perception more generally.

findings.source: 1. Background
findings.quote: glancing illumination angles make surfaces appear rougher than frontal illumination.

findings.consequent: Distinction between opaque reflectance and sub-surface scattering (perceived translucency)
findings.source: 1. Background
findings.quote: shadow regions are likely to play a role, as these are the portions of objects that are most affected by light that has passed through the object.

findings.antecedent: Contrast and blur of non-specular components of an object
findings.source: 1. Background
findings.quote: varying the contrast (both magnitude and sign) and blur of the non-specular components of an object can dramatically alter its appearance from diffuse to translucent.

findings.antecedent: Object thickness and distance to background
findings.consequent: Judgments of refractive index of solid transparent materials
findings.source: 1. Background
findings.quote: subjects could match the refractive index of solid transparent materials, although... their judgments were substantially biased by the thickness of the object and the distance to the background.

findings.source: 2. Computational goals and challenges of material perception
findings.quote: Estimating material properties (glossiness, roughness, colour, etc.) is likely to be a key stage in establishing the feature space within which samples can be categorized.

findings.source: 2. Computational goals and challenges of material perception
findings.quote: knowing which class a material belongs to presumably helps infer its properties.

findings.antecedent: Enormous within-class variability of material appearance
findings.source: 2.1. Material categorization
findings.quote: material categorization presents the visual system with the significant challenge of enormous within-class variability.

findings.source: 2.3. What makes material perception difficult?
findings.quote: the image of a given material can change dramatically depending on the context... the visual system cannot recognize materials by simply matching the image against a stored 'template'.

findings.antecedent: Image ambiguity (identical materials -> different images; different materials -> similar images)
findings.source: 2.3. What makes material perception difficult?
findings.quote: identical materials can create very different images, and very different materials can create surprisingly similar images.

findings.consequent: Estimation of physical properties (by discounting illumination/geometry)
findings.source: 3. Two theoretical approaches to material perception
findings.quote: inverse optics... the visual system explicitly estimates and 'discounts' the contributions of illumination and geometry to the observed intensity values

findings.consequent: Reconstruction of scene physics (light sources, geometry, reflectance)
findings.source: 3. Two theoretical approaches to material perception
findings.quote: visual system 'runs physics in reverse' to accurately model the physical properties of the scene, reconstructing the positions of light sources, the surface geometry and the physical reflectance parameters of the scene from the image.

findings.antecedent: A priori assumptions in inverse optics models
findings.consequent: Tractability of problem, but limited recovery of properties
findings.source: 3. Two theoretical approaches to material perception
findings.quote: To get around this problem, inverse optics models often invoke various kinds of a priori assumptions about the properties of the world... This makes the problem tractable, but limits the range of viewing conditions and physical properties that can be recovered from the image.

findings.antecedent: Image measurements invariant across illumination changes
findings.source: 3. Two theoretical approaches to material perception
findings.quote: identify image measurements that are diagnostic of material properties, but which remain roughly invariant across changes in the illumination... visual system could use these measurements to recognize the material.

findings.source: 3. Two theoretical approaches to material perception
findings.quote: when the spheres were rendered under illuminations that were photographically captured from the real world... subjects were quite good at performing the matches. By contrast, when the spheres were illuminated under unnatural illuminations... performance decreased significantly.

findings.source: 4. An alternative view of material perception as 'statistical appearance models'
findings.quote: changing the illumination can also affect the perceived glossiness of surfaces.

findings.source: 4. An alternative view of material perception as 'statistical appearance models'
findings.quote: when asked to estimate the glossiness of the surface, the judgments varied significantly depending on the depth of the relief.

findings.antecedent: Interactions between surface relief, reflectance, and illumination orientation
findings.source: 4. An alternative view of material perception as 'statistical appearance models'
findings.quote: the interactions between the factors were not only large, they were in some cases non-monotonic, which suggests that the effect is not a simple 'contamination' of one quantity (perceived glossiness) by another (relief)

findings.source: 4. An alternative view of material perception as 'statistical appearance models'
findings.quote: when subjects are asked to report the apparent glossiness of a surface, it could be that their judgments reflect the extent to which the surface manifests salient specular reflections.

findings.antecedent: Low-level image properties of highlights (size, contrast, distinctness)
findings.source: 4. An alternative view of material perception as 'statistical appearance models'
findings.quote: a simple weighted combination of these latter judgments [image properties of highlights] accounted for all the main trends in the glossiness judgments, including the non-monotonic effects of surface relief and the interactions between relief and illumination direction.

findings.source: 4.1. Statistical appearance models
findings.quote: the brain is highly adept at inferring a type of generative model of material appearance—a 'statistical appearance model'—which captures the natural degrees of variation between samples in terms of easily measured appearance properties.

findings.consequent: Parsing image into salient features (highlights, shadows)
findings.source: 4.2. How might statistical appearance models be computed?
findings.quote: the visual system first uses general-purpose perceptual organization mechanisms to parse the image into salient regions or features, such as the highlights and shadows across the surface.

findings.consequent: Explanation of perceptual phenomena (e.g., errors, non-intuitive effects)
findings.source: 5. Theoretical benefits of statistical appearance models
findings.quote: statistical appearance models also predict several perceptual phenomena that would otherwise be difficult to understand if the visual system's goal were to estimate physical properties of surfaces.

findings.consequent: Degree of spatial distortion of background patterns
findings.source: 5.3. Predicting systematic estimation errors and other eccentricities of material perception
findings.quote: The degree of distortion depends on the refractive index, a physical parameter of the material that determines how light is 'bent' as it passes through the object.

findings.antecedent: 3D thickness of refracting object, distance to background
findings.source: 5.3. Predicting systematic estimation errors and other eccentricities of material perception
findings.quote: the degree of distortion also varies with other scene variables, including the 3D thickness of the refracting object, as well as its distance from the background that is visible through it.

findings.antecedent: Object thickness or distance to background
findings.source: 5.3. Predicting systematic estimation errors and other eccentricities of material perception
findings.quote: subjects' matches [of refractive index] were substantially biased by the thickness or distance of the object, even though these scene variables have nothing to do with the intrinsic properties of the material.

findings.antecedent: Visual system matching image distortion (rather than estimating physical refractive index)
findings.consequent: Understanding of perceptual biases in refractive index judgments
findings.source: 5.3. Predicting systematic estimation errors and other eccentricities of material perception
findings.quote: if instead of estimating the physical refractive index of the transparent objects, subjects simply match the degree of distortion observable in the image... these biases can be easily understood.

findings.antecedent: Goal of color perception as estimating physical spectra
findings.source: 5.3. Predicting systematic estimation errors and other eccentricities of material perception
findings.quote: If the goal of colour perception were to estimate the physical spectra of sources or surfaces... then this circularity [of hue] makes no sense: why should hue be a circular dimension when wavelength is a linear dimension?

findings.source: 5.3. Predicting systematic estimation errors and other eccentricities of material perception
findings.quote: statistical appearance models are easier to compute than physical models, and more expressive than simple heuristics.

findings.consequent: Capture of sample characteristics and relationships (including novel samples)
findings.source: 5.3. Predicting systematic estimation errors and other eccentricities of material perception
findings.quote: Such models capture not only the key characteristics of individual samples, but also the relationships between samples, including novel samples that have not been seen before, by representing a material's natural dimensions of variation.

findings.consequent: Account for baffling effects of irrelevant scene variables
findings.source: 5.3. Predicting systematic estimation errors and other eccentricities of material perception
findings.quote: Appearance-based (rather than physics-based) explanations of material perception account for the otherwise baffling effects of irrelevant scene variable on material perception.

findings.consequent: General perceptual/cognitive faculty for inferring statistical regularities
findings.source: 5.4. Beyond material perception
findings.quote: the visual characterization of material appearance is likely to be just a special case of a much more general perceptual and cognitive faculty for inferring statistical regularities related to the high-level attributes of things, scenes and events.

limitations: It remains unclear at what level the constraints on perceptual organization mechanisms are imposed, and how additional grouping processes beyond raw filter responses and intensity statistics are involved.
A considerable amount of research is still needed to understand how perceptual organization mechanisms segment images into diffuse and specular reflections.

The proposed 'statistical appearance model' is highly speculative, and many questions remain regarding how segmentation processes work, how the visual system learns initial hypotheses, and how new evidence is incorporated into the model.
It is difficult to experimentally address the teleological question of the visual system's 'goal'.
Future research must test the ability of hypothesized cues to predict both successes and failures of material perception.
Methods need to be developed for perturbing image properties and measuring perceptual consequences to establish causal roles.
Theory must be developed to model how the visual system selects specific cues for material perception tasks.
It is crucial to understand not only which cues are used, but also how the visual system ends up using those cues over others.
Material perception research should avoid becoming a 'theory-blind process of collecting large numbers of weak correlations'.
minimum_safe_summary: This paper proposes a general theory of visual material perception, suggesting that the visual system does not estimate physical parameters directly but rather builds 'statistical generative models' of material appearance. These models capture natural variations in appearance based on easily measured image properties, such as the size, contrast, and distinctness of specular reflections for glossiness. Key findings indicate that human observers are adept at recognizing and categorizing materials from brief presentations, and that perceived material properties like glossiness and translucency are systematically affected by illumination statistics, surface relief, and object geometry. The theory explains perceptual errors and non-intuitive interactions between scene variables as a consequence of the visual system relying on statistical regularities rather than inverse physics. Limitations include the speculative nature of the proposal, the need for further research into perceptual organization mechanisms, and the challenge of experimentally addressing the visual system's ultimate 'goal' in material perception.
